title: Constructing Two Increasing Arrays
statement:
The arrays `nums1` and `nums2` hold only `0`s and `1`s, and `nums1` may be empty. Replace every `0` with an even positive integer and every `1` with an odd positive integer so that:

- each array becomes strictly increasing, and
- no integer is used more than once across the two arrays.

Return the smallest possible value of the largest integer used.
constraints: Every value of nums1 and nums2 is 0 or 1
notes:
## Intuition

Every integer is used once, so writing all of them in increasing order merges the two arrays: some interleaving of `nums1` and `nums2` in which the values climb strictly. For one fixed interleaving the best choice is greedy: give each element the smallest integer above the previous one that has the right parity. Trying every interleaving is exponential, but the best largest-so-far depends only on how many elements of each array have been placed, so a two-sequence DP over the prefixes of both arrays covers every interleaving at once.

## Approach

1. `dp[i][j]` is the smallest possible largest integer after placing the first `i` elements of `nums1` and the first `j` of `nums2`; `dp[0][0] = 0`.
2. `nextAbove(value, bit)` is the smallest integer above `value` with parity `bit`: `value + 1` if that fits, otherwise `value + 2`.
3. Row 0 places `nums2` alone and column 0 places `nums1` alone, each element taking `nextAbove` of the one before it.
4. In any other cell the last integer belongs to `nums1[i - 1]` (`viaNums1`, built on `dp[i - 1][j]`) or to `nums2[j - 1]` (`viaNums2`, built on `dp[i][j - 1]`); keep the smaller. Keeping only the smallest value per cell is safe because `nextAbove` never decreases when its input grows.
5. Return `dp[m][n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums1 = []` and `nums2 = [1,0,1,1]`, so `m = 0` and only row 0 is filled: `dp[0][1] = 1` (first odd), `dp[0][2] = 2` (even above 1), `dp[0][3] = 3`, and `dp[0][4] = 5` because 4 is even. The answer is `5`, from `[1, 2, 3, 5]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m·n): each of the (m + 1)(n + 1) cells takes O(1).
- Space: O(m·n) for the table; one row would do, since a cell reads only the row above and its left neighbour.

## Pitfalls

- Always serving whichever array's next element can take the smaller integer fails: for `nums1 = [1,0,0]`, `nums2 = [1,0,1]` it ends at 7 or 8 depending on how ties go, but `[3,4,6]` and `[1,2,5]` end at 6.
- The new integer must be strictly above the previous one: after 3, a `1` needs 5, not 3.
- `nums1` can be empty, so the table may have a single row.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m`, `n` | lengths of `nums1` and `nums2` |
| `nextAbove` | smallest integer above a value whose parity matches a bit |
| `dp[i][j]` | least possible largest integer after placing `i` elements of `nums1` and `j` of `nums2` |
| `i`, `j` | how many elements of each array are placed |
| `viaNums1`, `viaNums2` | the largest integer when `nums1[i - 1]`, or `nums2[j - 1]`, is placed last |

narration.4: nextAbove(value, bit) is the smallest integer above value that is odd when bit is 1 and even when bit is 0.
narration.5: dp[i][j] will be the least possible largest integer after placing i elements of nums1 and j of nums2; dp[0][0] = 0 as nothing is placed.
narration.6: Row 0: only elements of nums2 are placed.
narration.7: Each one takes the smallest fitting integer above the one before it.
narration.9: Now place the first i elements of nums1, for i from 1 to m.
narration.10: Column 0: only elements of nums1 are placed, chained the same way.
narration.11: Combine them with the first j elements of nums2.
narration.12: If nums1[i - 1] is placed last, it takes the smallest fitting integer above the best for (i - 1, j).
narration.13: If nums2[j - 1] is placed last, it takes the smallest fitting integer above the best for (i, j - 1).
narration.14: Either order is allowed, so keep whichever ends lower.
narration.17: Both arrays are fully placed: this is the smallest possible largest integer.
